t: Maximum Energy Boost From Two Drinks
o:
## Understanding the problem

Drink exactly one beverage per hour for n hours; boosts are energyDrinkA[i] / energyDrinkB[i]. Switching drinks costs the NEXT hour entirely (no boost that hour). Start with either drink; maximize total boost.

Example 1 `[1,3,1]` / `[3,1,1]`: sticking to one drink gives 1+3+1 = 5; any switch wastes an hour worth at most 3 but the pattern can't beat 5. Example 2 `[4,1,1]` / `[1,1,3]`: A at hour 0 (4), switch (waste hour 1), B at hour 2 (3) → 7, beating 4+1+1 = 6.

This is a two-state DP: let a[i] = best total through hour i given we drink A at hour i, b[i] similarly for B. Staying: a[i] = A[i] + a[i−1]. Switching from B: we must have drunk B at hour i−2 and idled at i−1, so a[i] = A[i] + b[i−2] (with b[−1] treated as 0, covering 'start fresh at hour i'). Symmetric for b.
k: Two-state linear DP: a[i] = A[i] + max(a[i−1], b[i−2]); b[i] = B[i] + max(b[i−1], a[i−2]).
The switch transition looks back TWO hours because the switch hour itself yields nothing.
Only the last two DP values are needed → O(1) rolling space.

a.i: Carry (a_{i−1}, b_{i−1}) and (a_{i−2}, b_{i−2}) as four scalars. At each hour compute the new pair from the recurrence, then shift. Answer is max of the final pair. Every schedule — stay, switch with a wasted hour, restart mid-way — is covered by the max over {stay, switch} transitions.
s: Initialize a = A[0], b = B[0], and previous-two values pa = pb = 0.
For i = 1..n−1: na = A[i] + max(a, pb); nb = B[i] + max(b, pa); then pa,pb = a,b; a,b = na,nb.
a.t: O(n) — single pass with constant work per hour.

a.n: Approach 2: Full DP arrays (clearer, same recurrence)
a.i: Materialize dp arrays of length n for pedagogical clarity; identical recurrence but easier to debug and extend (e.g., if you later need to reconstruct the actual schedule). Uses O(n) memory, which is fine for n ≤ 10⁵.
s: For i ≥ 1: dpA[i] = A[i] + max(dpA[i−1], i ≥ 2 ? dpB[i−2] : 0); dpB[i] symmetric.
a.t: O(n) — one pass over the arrays.
a.sp: O(n) for the two DP arrays.

w:
## Wrap-up

Present the array version first (easy to reason about), then note the O(1) rolling optimization. Pitfalls: looking back only one hour for switches (forgetting the wasted hour), mishandling i = 1 where the i−2 term doesn't exist, and 32-bit overflow of totals (up to 10⁵·10⁵ = 10¹⁰ — use 64-bit). Follow-up: three drinks, or a switch cost of k idle hours (generalize the lookback).
